sources.evidenceText: Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California, in Silicon Valley, and known for consumer electronics, software and online services. Founded in 1976 as Apple Computer Company by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, the company was incorporated by Jobs and Wozniak as Apple Computer, Inc. the following year. Its current name was adopted in 2007 as the company expanded its focus from computers to consumer electronics. Apple is one of the Big Tech companies. The company was founded to market Wozniak's Apple I computer. Its successor, the Apple II, became one of the first successful mass-produced personal microcomputers. Apple introduced the Lisa in 1983 and the Macintosh in 1984, popularizing graphical user interfaces navigated by a mouse. By 1985, internal conflicts led to Jobs leaving the company to form NeXT and Wozniak stepping back from active employment. During the 1990s, Apple lost considerable market share to lower-priced Wintel computers, Intel-powered PC clones running Windows. By 1997, Apple was reporting major losses and struggling to deliver a modernized operating system, leading it to acquire NeXT, which brought Jobs back to the company. Under his leadership, Apple returned to profitability through the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad, the iTunes Store, the Apple Store retail chain, and the "Think different" advertising campaign. Jobs resigned in 2011 for health reasons and died later that year. He was succeeded as CEO by Tim Cook, who will be succeeded by John Ternus in September 2026. Apple's product lineup includes portable and home hardware like the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods; several in-house operating systems such as iOS, iPadOS, and macOS; and various software and services including Apple Pay and iCloud, as well as multimedia streaming services like Apple Music and Apple TV. Since 2011, Apple has for the most part been the world's largest company by market capitalization, and, as of 2024, is the largest manufacturing company by revenue, the fourth-largest PC vendor, the largest vendor of tablet computers, and the largest vendor of mobile phones. Apple became the first publicly traded US company to be valued at over $1 trillion in 2018, and, as of October 2025, is valued at just over $4 trillion. Apple has received criticism regarding its contractors' labor conditions, its relationship with trade unions, its environmental practices, and its corporate ethics, including anti-competitive tactics, materials sourcing, and its acquisitions of smaller businesses. Nevertheless, the company has a large following and enjoys a high level of customer loyalty. Apple has consistently been ranked as one of the world's most valuable brands since the late 2000s.

sources.evidenceText: An apple is the round, edible fruit of an apple tree (Malus spp.). Fruit trees of the orchard or domestic apple (Malus domestica), the most widely grown in the genus, are cultivated worldwide. The tree originated in Central Asia, where its wild ancestor, Malus sieversii, is still found. Apples have been grown for thousands of years in Eurasia before they were introduced to North America by European colonists. Apples have cultural significance in many mythologies (including Norse and Greek) and religions (such as Christianity in Europe). Apples grown from seeds tend to be very different from those of their parents, and the resultant fruit frequently lacks desired characteristics. For commercial purposes, including botanical evaluation, apple cultivars are propagated by clonal grafting onto rootstocks. Apple trees grown without rootstocks tend to be larger and much slower to fruit after planting. Rootstocks are used to control the speed of growth and the size of the resulting tree, allowing for easier harvesting. There are more than 7,500 cultivars of apples. Different cultivars are bred for various tastes and uses, including cooking, eating raw, and cider or apple juice production. Trees and fruit are prone to fungal, bacterial, and pest problems, which can be controlled by a number of organic and non-organic means. In 2010, the fruit's genome was sequenced as part of research on disease control and selective breeding in apple production.

sources.evidenceText: Narendra Damodardas Modi (born 17 September 1950) is an Indian politician who has served as the prime minister of India since 26 May 2014. Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat from 2001 to 2014 and is the Member of Parliament (MP) for Varanasi. He is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a right-wing Hindutva paramilitary volunteer organisation. He is India's third-longest-serving prime minister, and the longest-serving prime minister outside the Indian National Congress. Modi was born and raised in Vadnagar, where he completed his secondary education. He was introduced to the RSS at the age of eight, becoming a full-time worker for the organisation in Gujarat in 1971. Assigned by the RSS to the BJP in 1985, he rose through the party hierarchy and became general secretary in 1998. In 2001, Modi was appointed chief minister of Gujarat and elected to the legislative assembly soon after. His administration is considered complicit in the 2002 Gujarat violence in which over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims, were killed, with many others raped or mutilated. An investigation authorised by the Supreme Court found no evidence to prosecute Modi. While his policies as chief minister were credited for encouraging economic growth, business and investment, his administration was criticised for failing to significantly improve health, poverty and education indices in the state. In the 2014 Indian general election, Modi led the BJP to a parliamentary majority, the first for a party since 1984. His administration increased direct foreign investment and reduced spending on healthcare, education, and social welfare. Modi began a high-profile sanitation campaign, introduced the Goods and Services Tax, and weakened or abolished environmental and labour laws. His demonetisation of banknotes in 2016 sparked controversy. A 2019 airstrike against an alleged terrorist camp in Pakistan failed to hit targets of significance but had nationalist appeal. After winning a second term in 2019, Modi's administration revoked the special status of Jammu and Kashmir. The same year it introduced the Citizenship Amendment Act, prompting widespread protests and spurring the 2020 Delhi riots in which Muslims were targeted by Hindu mobs. Three controversial farm laws led to widespread protests by farmers, eventually causing their repeal. Modi oversaw India's response to the COVID-19 pandemic which, according to the WHO, killed 4.7 million Indians. In the 2024 general election, the BJP lost its majority in the lower house of Parliament and formed a government leading a coalition. In Modi's third term, a terrorist attack in Pahalgam led to a military conflict with Pakistan, which resulted in a ceasefire. Under Modi's tenure, India has experienced democratic backsliding, or the weakening of democratic institutions, individual rights, and freedom of expression. As prime minister, he has received consistently high approval ratings. Modi has been described as engineering a political realignment towards right-wing politics. He remains a controversial figure domestically and internationally, over his Hindu nationalist beliefs and handling of the Gujarat violence, which have been cited as evidence of a majoritarian and exclusionary social agenda.

sources.evidenceText: The Sun is the star located at the centre of the Solar System. It is a massive sphere of hot plasma, heated to incandescence by nuclear fusion reactions in its core, radiating the energy from its surface mainly as visible light and infrared radiation with 10% at ultraviolet energies. It is the main source of energy for life on Earth. The Sun has been an object of veneration in many cultures and a central subject of astronomical research since antiquity. The Sun orbits the Galactic Center at a distance of 24,000 to 28,000 light-years. Its mean distance from Earth is about 1.496×108 kilometres or about 8 light-minutes. The distance between the Sun and the Earth was used to define a unit of length called the astronomical unit (au), now defined to be 149.5978707×106 kilometres. It is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System; its diameter is about 1,391,400 km (864,600 mi), around 109 times that of Earth. The Sun's mass is around 330,000 times that of Earth, making up about 99.86% of the total mass of the Solar System. The mass of the Sun's surface layer, its photosphere, consists mostly of hydrogen (~73%) and helium (~25%), with much smaller quantities of heavier elements, including oxygen, carbon, neon, and iron. The Sun formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a region of a large molecular cloud. Most of this matter gathered in the centre; the rest flattened into an orbiting disk that became the Solar System. The central mass became so hot and dense that it eventually initiated nuclear fusion in its core. It is now classified as a G-type main-sequence star (G2V). Every second, the Sun's core fuses about 600 billion kilograms (kg) of hydrogen into helium and converts four billion kilograms of matter into energy. About four to seven billion years from now, when hydrogen fusion in the Sun's core diminishes to the point where the Sun is no longer in hydrostatic equilibrium, its core will undergo a marked increase in density and temperature which will cause its outer layers to expand, eventually transforming the Sun into a red giant. After the red giant phase, models suggest the Sun will shed its outer layers and become a dense type of cooling star (a white dwarf), and no longer produce energy by fusion, but will still glow and give off heat from its previous fusion for perhaps trillions of years. After that, it is theorised to become an extremely dense black dwarf, giving off negligible energy.

sources.snippet: The degree Celsius is the unit of temperature on the Celsius temperature scale, one of two temperature scales used in the International System of Units (SI), the other being the closely related Kelvin scale. sources.evidenceText: The degree Celsius is the unit of temperature on the Celsius temperature scale, one of two temperature scales used in the International System of Units (SI), the other being the closely related Kelvin scale. The degree Celsius can refer to a specific point on the Celsius temperature scale or to a difference or range between two temperatures. It is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius (1701–1744), who proposed the first version of it in 1742. The unit was called centigrade in several languages for many years. In 1948, the International Committee for Weights and Measures renamed it to honor Celsius and also to remove confusion with the term for one hundredth of a gradian in some languages. Most countries use this scale, with the exception of the United States, some island territories, and Liberia, where the Fahrenheit scale is still used.

sources.evidenceText: Narendra Damodardas Modi (born 17 September 1950) is an Indian politician who has served as the prime minister of India since 26 May 2014. Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat from 2001 to 2014 and is the Member of Parliament (MP) for Varanasi. He is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a right-wing Hindutva paramilitary volunteer organisation. He is India's third-longest-serving prime minister, and the longest-serving prime minister outside the Indian National Congress. Modi was born and raised in Vadnagar, where he completed his secondary education. He was introduced to the RSS at the age of eight, becoming a full-time worker for the organisation in Gujarat in 1971. Assigned by the RSS to the BJP in 1985, he rose through the party hierarchy and became general secretary in 1998. In 2001, Modi was appointed chief minister of Gujarat and elected to the legislative assembly soon after. His administration is considered complicit in the 2002 Gujarat violence in which over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims, were killed, with many others raped or mutilated. An investigation authorised by the Supreme Court found no evidence to prosecute Modi. While his policies as chief minister were credited for encouraging economic growth, business and investment, his administration was criticised for failing to significantly improve health, poverty and education indices in the state. In the 2014 Indian general election, Modi led the BJP to a parliamentary majority, the first for a party since 1984. His administration increased direct foreign investment and reduced spending on healthcare, education, and social welfare. Modi began a high-profile sanitation campaign, introduced the Goods and Services Tax, and weakened or abolished environmental and labour laws. His demonetisation of banknotes in 2016 sparked controversy. A 2019 airstrike against an alleged terrorist camp in Pakistan failed to hit targets of significance but had nationalist appeal. After winning a second term in 2019, Modi's administration revoked the special status of Jammu and Kashmir. The same year it introduced the Citizenship Amendment Act, prompting widespread protests and spurring the 2020 Delhi riots in which Muslims were targeted by Hindu mobs. Three controversial farm laws led to widespread protests by farmers, eventually causing their repeal. Modi oversaw India's response to the COVID-19 pandemic which, according to the WHO, killed 4.7 million Indians. In the 2024 general election, the BJP lost its majority in the lower house of Parliament and formed a government leading a coalition. In Modi's third term, a terrorist attack in Pahalgam led to a military conflict with Pakistan, which resulted in a ceasefire. Under Modi's tenure, India has experienced democratic backsliding, or the weakening of democratic institutions, individual rights, and freedom of expression. As prime minister, he has received consistently high approval ratings. Modi has been described as engineering a political realignment towards right-wing politics. He remains a controversial figure domestically and internationally, over his Hindu nationalist beliefs and handling of the Gujarat violence, which have been cited as evidence of a majoritarian and exclusionary social agenda.

sources.evidenceText: The 2005 Atlantic hurricane season was a record-breaking, catastrophic, and deadly Atlantic hurricane season. It is the second-costliest hurricane season, just behind the 2017 season. It featured 28 tropical and subtropical storms, which was previously the most recorded in a hurricane season until the 2020 season. The United States National Hurricane Center named 27 storms, exhausting the annual pre-designated list, requiring the use of six Greek letter names, and adding an additional unnamed subtropical storm during a post-season re-analysis. A record 15 storms attained hurricane status, with maximum sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour (119 km/h). Of those, a record seven became major hurricanes, rated Category 3 or higher on the Saffir–Simpson scale. Four storms of this season became Category 5 hurricanes, the most of any season on record.

sources.evidenceText: The Eiffel Tower ( EYE-fəl; French: Tour Eiffel [tuʁ ɛfɛl] ) is a lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889. Locally nicknamed "La dame de fer" (French for "Iron Lady") for its use of wrought iron, it was constructed as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair, and to crown the centennial anniversary of the French Revolution. Although initially criticised by some of France's leading artists and intellectuals for its design, it has since become a global cultural icon of France and one of the most recognisable structures in the world. The tower received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022. The Eiffel Tower is the most visited monument with an entrance fee in the world: 6.91 million people ascended it in 2015. It was designated a monument historique in 1964, and was named part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991. The tower is 330 metres (1,083 ft) tall, about the same height as an 81-storey building, and the tallest structure in Paris. Its base is square, measuring 125 metres (410 ft) on each side. During its construction, the Eiffel Tower surpassed the Washington Monument to become by far the tallest human-made structure in the world, a title it held for 41 years until the Chrysler Building in New York City was finished in 1930. It was the first structure in the world to surpass both the 200-metre and 300-metre mark in height. Due to the addition of a broadcasting aerial at the top of the tower in 1957, it is now taller than the Chrysler Building by 11 metres (36 ft). Excluding transmitters, the Eiffel Tower is the second tallest free-standing structure in France after the Millau Viaduct. The tower has three levels for visitors, with restaurants on the first and second levels. The top level's upper platform is 276 m (906 ft) above the ground—the highest public observation deck in the European Union. Tickets can be purchased to ascend by stairs or lift to the first and second levels. The climb from ground level to the first level is over 300 steps, as is the climb from the first level to the second, making the entire ascent a 600-step climb. Although there is a staircase to the top level, it is usually accessible only by lift. On this top, third level, is a private apartment built for Gustave Eiffel, who decorated it with furniture made by Jean Lachaise and invited friends such as Thomas Edison.

56 years ago (1970-08-12)StadiumParc des PrincesCapacity47,929Owner(s)Qatar Sports Investments (85.9%)Arctos Partners (12.5%)Boardroom (1.6%)PresidentNasser Al-KhelaifiHead coachLuis EnriqueLeagueLigue 12025–26Ligue 1, 1st of 18 (champions)WebsitePSG.FR Home colours Away colours Current season Active departments ofParis Saint-Germain Football(Men's)Football(Youth Mixed)Football(Women's)Handball(Men's)EsportsJudo(Mixed) Closed departments ofParis Saint-Germain Basketball(Men's)Volleyball(Men's)Boxing(Men's)Rugby League(Men's) Paris Saint-Germain Football Club, commonly referred to as Paris Saint-Germain ( French: [paʁi sɛ̃ʒɛʁmɛ̃]), PSG, Paris, or Paris SG, is a French professional football club based in Paris. Founded in 1970 through the merger of Paris FC and Stade Saint-Germain, the club competes in Ligue 1, the highest division of French football, and plays its home matches at the Parc des Princes. PSG is France's most widely supported football club and one of the most followed clubs worldwide. The club has rivalries with Olympique de Marseille, against whom it contests Le Classique, and Paris FC in the Paris derby. With 61 official trophies, including 60 major honours, PSG is the most successful club in French football. The club has won a record 14 Ligue 1 titles, one Ligue 2 title, a record 16 Coupes de France, a record 9 Coupes de la Ligue, and a record 14 Trophée des Champions. Internationally, PSG is the most decorated French club, having won six major trophies: a French-record two UEFA Champions League titles, the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup, two UEFA Super Cup, the UEFA Intertoto Cup, and the FIFA Intercontinental Cup. Before the Qatar Sports Investments (QSI) takeover of PSG in 2011, the club had won 18 major trophies, including one UEFA Cup Winners' Cup, two Ligue 1 titles and eight Coupes de France, making it the joint third-most successful club in French football at the time. After the acquisition by QSI, the club entered a period of sustained domestic dominance, attracting numerous high-profile players and becoming the country's most successful club. The club won its first UEFA Champions League title in 2025 as part of a continental treble before successfully defending the trophy in 2026. Since 2011, PSG has been majority-owned by Qatar Sports Investments, with Arctos Partners acquiring a minority stake in 2023 and Boardroom in 2025. As of January 2026, the club is the wealthiest in France and ranks among the richest and most valuable football clubs in the world. In addition to its men's football team, PSG operates a youth academy, a women's football team, and sections in handball, judo, and esports. The club has also previously fielded teams in basketball, volleyball, boxing, and rugby league. History Main article: History of Paris Saint-Germain FC PSG regained prominence thanks to the Qatari takeover in 2011 and high-profile signings such as Neymar. Paris Saint-Germain were founded in 1970 following the merger of Paris FC and Stade Saint-Germain. PSG made an immediate impact, winning Ligue 2 and thus achieving promotion to Ligue 1 in their first season. PSG's momentum was soon halted, and the club split in 1972. Paris FC remained in the top flight, while PSG were relegated to Division 3. After two consecutive promotions, PSG quickly returned to the top flight in 1974 and moved to the Parc des Princes.[1][2][3][4][5] The club's first trophies arrived in the 1980s. Led by players such as Safet Sušić, Luis Fernandez and Dominique Rocheteau, the Parisians claimed back-to-back Coupe de France in 1982 and 1983, and their first Ligue 1 title in 1986. A steep decline followed, but the takeover by Canal+ in 1991 revitalized PSG. Led by David Ginola, George Weah and Raí, the club won nine trophies and reached five consecutive European semi-finals during the 1990s. Notably, Paris captured their second league title in 1994 and the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup in 1996, with the legendary Luis Fernandez now as manager.[2][3][4][5][6][7] At the beginning of the 21st century, the Parisians were struggling to get back to the top despite the magic of Ronaldinho and the goals of Pauleta. Five more trophies followed: three Coupe de France, a Coupe de la Ligue and a UEFA Intertoto Cup, but PSG became better known for struggling through one crisis after another. Inevitably, Canal+ sold the club to Colony Capital in 2006. However, the situation only worsened, and PSG spent the next two seasons avoiding relegation.[2][3][4][5] The club's fortunes changed dramatically with the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments, operated by the government of Qatar, as owners in 2011. Since then, PSG have invested heavily in signings of world-class players such as Zlatan Ibrahimović, Lionel Messi, Neymar and Kylian Mbappé, the latter two being the most expensive transfers in football history. As a result, PSG have dominated French football, winning 38 trophies: twelve league titles, eight Coupe de France, six Coupe de la Ligue and twelve Trophée des Champions. They have also become a regular in the knockout stages of the UEFA Champions League, reaching the final for the first time in their history in 2020, winning their first title in 2025 as part of a continental treble, and retaining the title in 2026.[2][5][8][9][10][11] PSG also claimed the 2025 UEFA Super Cup and the 2025 FIFA Intercontinental Cup, achieving an unprecedented sextuple.[12][13][14] Identity Colours and mascot Germain the Lynx, the club's mascot. Since their foundation, Paris Saint-Germain have represented both the city of Paris and the nearby royal town of Saint-Germain-en-Laye.[5] As a result, red, blue and white are the club's traditional colours.[15] The red and blue are Parisian colours, a nod to revolutionary figures Lafayette and Jean Sylvain Bailly, and the white is a symbol of French royalty and Saint-Germain-en-Laye.[15][16] On the club's crest, the Eiffel Tower in red and the blue background represent Paris, while the fleur de lys in white is a hint to the coat of arms of Saint-Germain-en-Laye.[15][16] The fleur de lys is a royal symbol as well and recalls that French King Louis XIV was born in the town.[15] Throughout its history, PSG have brandished several crests, but all of them have featured the club's three historical colours.[17] Likewise, PSG's most distinctive shirts have been predominantly red, blue or white, with the remaining two colours included as well.[18] The club's official mascot, Germain the Lynx, also sports PSG's traditional colours.[16] It was unveiled during the 2010 Tournoi de Paris in commemoration of the club's 40th anniversary, and can be seen entertaining kids in the stands of the Parc des Princes or near the pitch with the players during the warm-up.[19] Anthems and mottos "Allez Paris!", recorded by Belgian actress and singer Annie Cordy in 1971, was the club's first official anthem. A dedicated PSG supporter from the very beginning, Cordy was part of an association of hundreds of celebrities who contributed to the club's founding in 1970. At that time, an appeal was made to the public to purchase season tickets at newsstands. A year later, Cordy was named PSG's official godmother and recorded the aforementioned anthem.[20][21] The club's second anthem, "Allez Paris‑Saint‑Germain!" by Les Parisiens, was recorded in 1977, replacing Annie Cordy's original version. It was produced and released by long-time PSG leader and music producer Charles Talar.[22][23][24] The chorus became a popular chant among PSG fans during matches.[25] A new version of the anthem, retaining the same title, was recorded in 2010 as part of the club's 40th anniversary celebrations. Performed to the tune of "Go West" by Village People, the lyrics were rewritten with input from the fans. This version serves as the club's current official anthem.[16][19][23] "Ô Ville Lumière", set to the tune of "Flower of Scotland", is another official club anthem for PSG fans.[26][27] This chant was created by the former KoB ultra group Boulogne Boys.[28] Other notable chants include "Le Parc est à nous" ("The Parc is ours"), "Ici, c'est Paris" ("This is Paris"), and "Paris est magique" ("Paris is magical").[25][29][30] "Who Said I Would" by English musician Phill Collins is also a traditional fan anthem. The song has accompanied the players' entrance onto the field since 1992. Collins was preceded by French singer Michel Fugain and his 1972 song "Attention, Ladies and Gentlemen."[31] "Ici, c'est Paris" and "Paris est magique" are also the club's most iconic mottos.[16][32][33] The "Ici, c'est Paris" slogan was created by the former VA ultra group Supras Auteuil, which registered it as a trademark in 2008.[30][34] PSG began incorporating the slogan into their marketing, resulting in a legal dispute with the Supras. In February 2016, the group rejected the club's offer of €2,000 for the rights to the slogan.[30] An agreement was reached in August 2019, allowing the club to continue using the slogan in advertising while fans retained the right to use it freely.[35] Iconic shirts Wikimedia Commons has media related to Paris Saint-Germain FC kits. For its first three seasons, Paris Saint-Germain's home shirt was red with blue and white detailing on the sleeves and collar to unify the club's three colours: the red and blue of Paris and the white of Saint-Germain-en-Laye.[18][36] During the 2010–11 season, PSG wore a red shirt for home matches to mark its 40th anniversary.[37] French fashion designer Daniel Hechter took over as president of PSG in 1973, and designed the club's traditional home kit that same year: a blue shirt with a red vertical stripe flanked by two thinner white stripes (blue–white–red–white–blue).[36][38] PSG's three most iconic shirts. First worn in the 1973–74 season, the so-called "Hechter shirt" has remained PSG's classic identity ever since.[18][39][40][41] The famous shirt was debuted against Red Star in November 1973.[42] This was also the club's first match at the Parc des Princes. PSG won 3–1 with Othniel Dossevi scoring the club's first goal in a Hechter shirt.[43] PSG stars from the 1990s and 2000s such as Raí, Ronaldinho and Pauleta are associated with this kit. In it, the club reached five consecutive European semi-finals between 1993 and 1997, lifted the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup in 1996 and achieved eight consecutive victories against arch-rivals Olympique de Marseille between 2002 and 2004.[18][44] It is commonly believed that Hechter based his design on the red-and-white jersey worn by Ajax, the dominant European club at the time.[36][38] Hechter himself denied

sources.evidenceText: Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with an estimated city population of 2.04 million in an area of 105.4 km2 (40.7 sq mi), and a metropolitan population of 13.2 million as of January 2026. Located on the river Seine in the centre of the Île-de-France region, it is the largest metropolitan area and fourth-most populous city in the European Union (EU). Paris is nicknamed the "City of Light", partly because of its role in the Age of Enlightenment. Administratively, Paris is divided into twenty arrondissements (districts), each having their own cultural identity. Haussmann's renovation of Paris, which created new boulevards, parks, and public works, gave birth to a modern city known as the "capital of the 19th century". Paris is a major railway, motorway, and air-transport hub; in 2024 Charles de Gaulle Airport was the EU's busiest airport. Paris has one of the most sustainable transportation systems in the world and is one of only two cities that have received the Sustainable Transport Award twice. Its Art Nouveau-decorated Métro has become a symbol of the city. Paris is known for its museums and architectural landmarks: the Musée d'Orsay, Musée Marmottan Monet, and Musée de l'Orangerie are noted for their collections of French Impressionist art, while the Musée National d'Art Moderne, Musée Rodin, and Musée Picasso are noted for their collections of modern and contemporary art. Parts of the city along the Seine have been designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The president of France and both houses of the French Parliament sit in Paris. Paris is home to several United Nations organisations, including UNESCO, as well as other international organisations such as the OECD, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (in neighbouring Saint-Cloud), the International Energy Agency, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the International Federation for Human Rights, and the Fédération internationale de l'Automobile, along with European bodies such as the European Space Agency, the European Banking Authority, and the European Securities and Markets Authority. The city hosts many sporting events, such as the French Open, and is the home of the association football club Paris Saint-Germain and the rugby union club Stade Français. Paris has also hosted the Summer Olympics three times, in 1900, 1924 and 2024.

sources.evidenceText: The Indian National Congress (INC), also known as the Congress Party, or simply the Congress, is a big tent political party in India. It is India's oldest existing political party and is widely regarded as one of the world's oldest continuously active political parties, outside Europe and North America. Founded on 28 December 1885, it was the first modern nationalist movement to emerge in the British Empire in Asia and Africa. From the late 19th century, and especially after 1920, under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, the Congress became the principal leader of the Indian independence movement. The Congress was one of the parties that led India to independence from the United Kingdom, and significantly influenced other anti-colonial nationalist movements in the British Empire.

sources.evidenceText: The degree Celsius is the unit of temperature on the Celsius temperature scale, one of two temperature scales used in the International System of Units (SI), the other being the closely related Kelvin scale. The degree Celsius can refer to a specific point on the Celsius temperature scale or to a difference or range between two temperatures. It is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius (1701–1744), who proposed the first version of it in 1742. The unit was called centigrade in several languages for many years. In 1948, the International Committee for Weights and Measures renamed it to honor Celsius and also to remove confusion with the term for one hundredth of a gradian in some languages. Most countries use this scale, with the exception of the United States, some island territories, and Liberia, where the Fahrenheit scale is still used.

sources.evidenceText: The chief minister of Tamil Nadu is the head of government of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu. In accordance with the Constitution of India, the governor is a state's de jure head, while the de facto authority rests with the chief minister. Following elections to the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly, the state's governor usually invites the party with the majority of seats in the assembly to form the government. The governor appoints the chief minister, whose council of ministers are collectively responsible to the assembly. Given that the chief minister has the confidence of the assembly, the chief minister's term is for five years and is subject to no term limits.

Fahrenheit vs. Celsius Benchmarks In the world of thermometry, the freezing point of water in fahrenheit is defined as exactly 32°F. On the metric scale, this same physical threshold is represented as 0°C, serving as a fundamental anchor for global temperature scales. This specific phase transition occurs when water molecules lose enough kinetic energy to stop flowing freely as a liquid. At the molecular level, hydrogen bonding begins to dominate as the temperature drops toward these benchmarks. These bonds pull the molecules into a geometric crystallization pattern known as a hexagonal lattice. As the liquid turns to ice, it releases latent heat, which keeps the temperature stable until the transition is entirely complete. The Role of Sea Level The temperature water freezes at sea level is the universal standard because atmospheric pressure directly influences molecular behavior. At 1 atmosphere of pressure, the physical properties of pure water are predictable and highly consistent. This baseline allows scientists and engineers to study thermodynamics without the interference of varying altitudes. When pressure remains constant at sea level, the transition from liquid to solid is a precise and repeatable event. Any deviation from these standard conditions can alter the energy required for crystallization to take hold. Understanding this benchmark is essential for calculating how water behaves in controlled laboratory environments versus the natural world. Beyond simple temperature readings, external factors like environment play a massive role in when ice begins to form.Variables That Change the Freezing Point Key Takeaway: Adding substances like salt or changing the pressure can significantly lower the temperature required for water to turn into ice. Impact of Impurities and Solutes Pure water molecules require a specific geometry to form a stable crystalline lattice. When solutes are introduced into the liquid, they cause molecular disruption by physically getting in the way of the hydrogen bonds. This interference results in a phenomenon known as freezing point depression, which forces the water to reach a much lower temperature before it can successfully transition into ice. Conversely, in a vacuum where pressure is nearly non-existent, water can boil and freeze simultaneously in a state known as the triple point. Anders Celsius and the Centigrade Scale In 1742, Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius introduced a temperature scale that was initially inverted compared to our modern version. sources.evidenceText: General Science & Chemistry What is the Temperature at Which Water Freezes? [The Real Science] April 9, 2026 · 8 minutes read Table of Contents The Standard Freezing Point: Fahrenheit vs. Celsius Historical Context of the 32 Degree Mark Global Standard Differences Variables That Shift the Freezing Point The Impact of Atmospheric Pressure The Role of Solutes and Impurities Supercooling and Rapid Phase Transition Nucleation Sites and Crystal Formation The Physics of Instant Ice Visualizing Phase Change: The Science of Ice Frequently Asked Questions Why does salt lower the freezing point? Can water stay liquid below 32 degrees? Does hot water freeze faster? Pure water freezes at exactly 32 degrees Fahrenheit (0 degrees Celsius) under standard atmospheric pressure. However, this seemingly fixed number shifts dramatically based on mineral content and environmental pressure. Understanding these variables is critical for everything from automotive maintenance to meteorology. Let's explore why this fundamental constant is more flexible than you think. Image taken from the YouTube channel minutephysics , from the video titled The Physics of Supercooling . The Standard Freezing Point: Fahrenheit vs. Celsius Key Takeaway: 32°F is the baseline for pure water at sea level, establishing the foundation for the Fahrenheit scale. These scales provide a universal language for thermal measurement. Under standard atmospheric pressure, pure water transitions from a liquid state to a solid state at 32°F or 0°C. This specific thermal threshold acts as a physical constant that anchors global meteorology and thermodynamics. While these numbers seem arbitrary, they represent the culmination of centuries of refinement in how we observe the physical world. Understanding these benchmarks is essential for navigating scientific data across different regions. Historical Context of the 32 Degree Mark Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit developed his namesake scale in the early 18th century, initially using a brine mixture to set his zero point. He eventually standardized the freezing point of pure water at 32 degrees to ensure clear, repeatable increments between freezing and the human body’s internal heat. This calibration provided the first reliable way to measure seasonal shifts and industrial processes. By setting the boiling point at 212 degrees, Fahrenheit created a 180-degree span that simplified many early mathematical models of heat transfer. While his original scale famously placed the boiling point at 0 and freezing at 100, it was later reversed to create the intuitive 0-to-100 system we recognize today. Global Standard Differences The Metric system currently dominates global scientific and civilian discourse, utilizing the Celsius scale for its logical base-10 structure. Most nations transitioned to this standard decades ago to simplify international trade and research protocols. The United States remains the most prominent user of Fahrenheit for daily weather and domestic applications. Navigating these various temperature scales requires a grasp of the NIST Guide on Temperature Units, which defines the precise relationship between Celsius, Fahrenheit, and the Kelvin scale used in physics. Standardized measurements at sea level provide the following benchmarks for pure water: Fahrenheit: Water freezes at exactly 32°F and boils at 212°F. Celsius: Water freezes at exactly 0°C and boils at 100°C. Kelvin: The thermodynamic freezing point is 273.15 K, where all molecular motion is referenced against absolute zero. Scale Freezing Point Boiling Point Celsius (°C) 0 100 Fahrenheit (°F) 32 212 Kelvin (K) 273.15 373.15 Beyond simple numbers, the chemistry of the water itself determines when crystallization begins.Variables That Shift the Freezing Point Key Takeaway: Adding solutes like salt or increasing pressure prevents water molecules from forming a stable hexagonal lattice. This phenomenon explains why the ocean remains liquid at temperatures that freeze fresh water. The standard 32°F benchmark serves as a baseline for pure water at sea level, but it is far from a universal law. Real-world environments introduce variables that disrupt the predictable transition from liquid to solid. Molecular bonds are highly sensitive to environmental shifts and chemical compositions. When these variables fluctuate, the thermal energy required to lock molecules into a crystalline structure changes significantly. The Impact of Atmospheric Pressure Pressure exerts a direct physical force that interferes with the expansion of water as it freezes. High hydrostatic pressure pushes molecules closer together, effectively counteracting the expansion needed for ice formation. In the deep ocean or high-pressure industrial systems, this force pushes the freezing point downward. Significant depth creates a physical barrier where water remains liquid well below its standard freezing threshold. Pressure (atm) Freezing Point (°C) Freezing Point (°F) 1 atm 0.00 32.00 500 atm -3.85 25.07 1,000 atm -8.00 17.60 While atmospheric pressure changes at higher elevations are negligible for freezing, extreme depths illustrate how force overrides temperature. Any substantial increase in pressure demands more cooling to achieve solidification. [The Truth] The Role of Solutes and Impurities Dissolving a substance into water triggers a chemical reaction known as freezing point depression. Foreign particles physically occupy space between water molecules, preventing them from aligning into a structured hexagonal lattice. High salinity is the primary driver behind oceanic resistance to ice. According to data from NOAA: Why Does the Ocean Freeze?, the presence of salt lowers the thermal threshold, requiring much colder environments to freeze seawater. This chemical interference often works in tandem with boiling point elevation. The same solutes that make it harder for water to freeze also make it more difficult for the liquid to transition into gas by lowering its vapor pressure. Sodium Chloride (Salt): The most common natural solute affecting the freezing point of water bodies. Ethylene Glycol: A synthetic chemical engineered to prevent freezing in automotive cooling systems. Magnesium Chloride: A highly effective brine used to lower the freezing point on frozen winter roads. Calcium Chloride: An industrial salt that works efficiently even in extreme sub-zero temperatures. Each of these substances introduces molecular chaos that opposes the order required for ice. By creating a physical barrier to crystallization, solutes ensure water stays in a liquid state longer than pure H2O. This molecular resistance leads to a fascinating state known as supercooling.Supercooling and Rapid Phase Transition Key Takeaway: Water can remain liquid down to -40°F if it lacks nucleation sites like dust or minerals. The introduction of a single catalyst triggers an immediate transition to a solid state. Pure water does not always turn into ice at the standard 32°F threshold. In a state known as supercooling, liquid water maintains its fluid form well below its nominal freezing point by avoiding the structural triggers required for solid formation. This phenomenon occurs because water molecules require a surface or a "seed" to begin the process of crystallization. Without these catalysts, the kinetic energy of the molecules remains sufficient to prevent the formation of a stable crystal lattice despite the plummeting temperature. This happens when impurities such as dust, bacteria, or mineral salts provide a structural template for ice crystals to latch onto and grow within the liquid. When water is ultra-pure, it bypasses these external triggers and remains liquid in sub-zero environments. The temperature must drop significantly lower—down to approximately -40°F—to achieve homogeneous nucleation. At this extreme thermal floor, the internal movement of the water molecules slows enough for them to align spontaneously. They form the necessary geometric clusters to bridge the gap between liquid and solid states without the assistance of any external impurities. The Physics of Instant Ice The transition from a supercooled liquid to a solid is nearly instantaneous once a physical disturbance occurs. Introducing a single ice crystal or even a sharp mechanical shock forces the unstable liquid to reorganize its molecular structure in seconds. As this rapid phase change occurs, the water releases latent heat into its immediate environment. This thermal energy surge actually warms the surrounding mixture, often bringing the remaining liquid back up toward the standard freezing point even as the ice mass expands. This "flash freeze" is a violent physical event where the latent energy stored in the liquid state is suddenly discharged. It represents one of the most dramatic phase shifts observable in common chemistry and demonstrates how temperature is only one part of the freezing equation. Achieving a stable supercooled state requires a specific set of environmental and physical parameters to prevent accidental solidification: Extreme molecular purity to eliminate potential heterogeneous nucleation points. A complete lack of mechanical vibration or sudden agitation. Highly controlled cooling rates that prevent localized temperature spikes or density shifts. Recognizing these scientific nuances is essential for accurate meteorological forecasting and industrial safety. These common questions address the nuances of the freezing process. Why does salt lower the freezing point? Salt ions physically disrupt the ability of water molecules to align into a rigid, hexagonal crystalline lattice. This phenomenon, known as freezing point depression, occurs because dissolved solute particles act as mechanical obstacles that block water molecules from bonding. To overcome this interference and achieve a solid state, the thermal energy must decrease significantly further, forcing the molecules to slow down enough to lock into place despite the presence of the salt. Can water stay liquid below 32 degrees? Pure water transitions into a supercooled state and remains liquid at temperatures as low as -40°F if it lacks nucleation sites. Ice crystallization requires a "seed" or impurity, such as dust or a container wall imperfection, to trigger the organization of molecules into a solid. In high-purity environments, water molecules cannot easily form the initial cluster needed to start the chain reaction of freezing, allowing the liquid to persist well below the standard freezing threshold. Does hot water freeze faster? The Mpemba effect describes a paradoxical scenario where hot water reaches its freezing point faster than cold water under specific environmental variables. High temperatures accelerate evaporation, which reduces the total mass of the liquid that must be cooled to reach the solid state. Furthermore, increased convection currents in hot water facilitate more rapid heat distribution and energy loss to the surroundings, potentially bypassing the cooling rate of initially colder, more stagnant water. While 32°F remains the standard benchmark, the physics of freezing is a dynamic process influenced by external forces. Mastering these variables allows for better control in industrial and domestic applications alike. The Freezing Point of Water in Celsius Key Takeaway: Under standard sea-level pressure, the freezing point of pure water is the primary benchmark for the Celsius scale at exactly 0 degrees. The Standard Definition The freezing point of water in celsius is defined as the temperature at which water transitions from a liquid to a solid state. This specific phase change occurs at exactly 0 degrees celsius water when the environment is held at standard atmospheric pressure. To ensure absolute precision, measurements are typically conducted at sea level. At this specific point, the liquid and solid phases exist in thermal equilibrium, meaning no net change in the state occurs unless energy is added or removed. Recommended Reading Coarse Echo Pattern: What Your Ultrasound Results Mean (Explained) It is important to note that the presence of impurities or changes in pressure can shift this value. However, for standard scientific and residential purposes, the value remains fixed at the zero mark. The Legacy of Anders Celsius The scale is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, who first proposed a centigrade system in 1742. His original design was actually the inverse of our modern system, with the boiling point at zero and the freezing point at one hundred. Following his tenure, the scale was reversed to the orientation used today to improve intuitive utility. This correction established the freezing point of water in celsius as a global anchor for thermodynamic and meteorological data. Beyond the basic number, the actual physical process involves a fascinating shift at the molecular level.The Physics Behind the 0°C Freeze Key Takeaway: Freezing is not just about temperature; it requires the release of latent heat to allow molecules to lock into a solid hexagonal lattice. A common point of inquiry among students and researchers is, does water freeze at 0 degrees exactly in every scenario? Under standard atmospheric pressure, 0°C serves as the critical equilibrium point where the liquid and solid phases of water coexist. Hydrogen Bonding As water cools toward the freezing point, the kinetic energy of individual molecules decreases. This reduction in molecular motion allows hydrogen bonds to become more stable and influential than the disruptive thermal energy. The molecules gradually align into a highly ordered crystalline structure. This arrangement results in a hexagonal lattice, a configuration that creates more space between molecules than is found in the liquid state. Latent Heat of Fusion The transition from liquid to solid is not instantaneous upon reaching 0°C. The substance must first release its latent heat, which is the internal energy required to break or form molecular bonds without changing the temperature. During this energy exchange, the water remains at a constant temperature until the phase change is complete. Additionally, the presence of nucleation sites, such as dust particles or surface irregularities, is typically necessary to initiate the crystallization process. While 0°C is the standard, several environmental factors can force water to stay liquid at much lower temperatures.Factors That Change the Freezing Point Key Takeaway: Impurities like salt and changes in pressure can significantly lower the temperature required for water to turn into ice. While 0°C is the standard reference, several water freezing point variables can alter this phase change threshold. These factors influence the molecular energy required to transition from a liquid state to a crystalline solid. Freezing Point Depression The introduction of solutes, such as salt or sugar, disrupts the formation of the hexagonal ice lattice. This phenomenon, known as freezing point depression, occurs because the dissolved particles interfere with water molecules' ability to bond together. Higher levels of salinity require a greater removal of thermal energy to achieve solidification. This is why seawater remains liquid at temperatures where fresh water would typically freeze solid. Common impurities in natural water sources often cause the liquid phase to persist well below 0°C. In specific laboratory settings, supercooling can also occur if the water is exceptionally pure and lacks nucleation sites to trigger ice formation. The Impact of Atmospheric Pressure Standard freezing points are generally measured at one atmosphere of pressure. Variations in altitude or artificial compression cause minute but measurable shifts in the temperature at which ice forms. The celsius to fahrenheit freezing point correlation is one of the most fundamental comparisons in thermodynamics. While the Celsius scale identifies the solidification of water at zero, the Fahrenheit scale identifies this same state at 32 degrees Fahrenheit. The Conversion Formula To bridge these two systems, a precise mathematical ratio is required. The conversion dictates that for every five units on the Celsius scale, there are nine units on the Fahrenheit scale. This ensures that 0 degrees Celsius is always mathematically equal to 32 degrees Fahrenheit under standard atmospheric conditions. Recommended Reading Cottage Cheese Cats: Is It Safe? (Vet-Approved Safety Guide) Why the Scales Differ The variance stems from different historical benchmarks used during the development of these systems. While the metric system eventually adopted the Celsius scale for its decimal-based logic, the Fahrenheit scale was originally built using different chemical reference points. In broader scientific contexts, neither scale represents the lowest possible energy state. Scientists often prefer Kelvin, which begins at absolute zero, to measure thermal energy without the use of negative integers. Frequently Asked Questions Is the freezing point of water always exactly 0 degrees Celsius? No, the freezing point of water can vary based on specific environmental factors. While 0°C is the standard at sea level, changes in atmospheric pressure can shift this temperature. Furthermore, the presence of impurities like salt or other dissolved solids will lower the freezing point through a process known as freezing point depression, meaning the water must reach a temperature colder than 0°C to solidify. Why does ice float if it is just frozen water? Ice floats because water is one of the few substances that expands and becomes less dense when it transitions from a liquid to a solid. As water reaches 0°C, its molecules form a rigid, hexagonal crystalline lattice that occupies more volume than the liquid state. Because the resulting ice is less dense than the liquid water beneath it, it remains buoyant and floats on the surface. What is the difference between the freezing point and the melting point? For pure water at standard pressure, the freezing point and melting point are identical at 0°C. The primary difference is the direction of the energy exchange. The freezing point refers to the temperature at which heat is being removed from the system to turn liquid into solid, whereas the melting point refers to the temperature at which heat is being added to turn solid ice back into liquid water. He is the son of the late Y S Rajasekhara Reddy, a former Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh. Following in his father’s footsteps, Jagan Mohan Reddy served as the 17th Chief Minister of the state. He is also the founder and President of the YSR Congress Party. Presently, he serves as a member of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly. Jagan Mohan Reddy Biography Yeduguri Sandinti Jagan Mohan Reddy, known as Y S Jaganmohan Reddy, is an Indian entrepreneur and politician. Born on December 21, 1972, in Pulivendula village of Kadapa District, Andhra Pradesh, he is the son of former Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Y S Rajasekhara Reddy, and Vijayalakshmi. Reddy received his education at The Hyderabad Public School and later pursued a Bachelor of Commerce degree from Pragathi Mahavidyalaya Degree and PG College, Ram Koti, Hyderabad. He furthered his studies in business management in the United States before returning to India to join his father's business. Reddy's political journey began when he campaigned for the Indian National Congress (INC) during the 2004 elections and was elected as the Member of Parliament (MP) from the Kadapa Lok Sabha constituency in 2009. Following his father's tragic demise in a helicopter crash in 2009, Reddy founded his own political party, the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP). In 2011, he embarked on a massive padayatra, covering approximately 3,000 km over 14 months, which bolstered his popularity and garnered widespread support. In 2019, Reddy led the YSRCP to a landslide victory in the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly elections, securing 151 out of 175 seats, and subsequently assuming the role of Chief Minister. His party also won 22 out of 25 Lok Sabha seats. Reddy's ascension to power marked a significant political shift in Andhra Pradesh, particularly given the decline of the Indian National Congress and the defeat of the Telugu Desam Party led by N Chandrababu Naidu. In his role as Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Reddy has introduced numerous welfare programs aimed at benefiting the state's residents. Among these initiatives are the 'Amma Vodi' scheme, offering financial aid to mothers who ensure their children attend school, and the 'Rythu Bharosa' scheme, providing financial support to farmers. These programs have garnered widespread popularity under his administration. A decade prior, Reddy was primarily engaged in business ventures in Bengaluru. However, at the behest of his father, he entered politics and contested the May 2009 Lok Sabha elections from the Kadapa constituency, despite lacking prior political experience. The unexpected passing of his father in September 2009 propelled Reddy into the political spotlight, with calls for him to assume the role of Chief Minister. In the 2024 Assembly elections, he successfully contested and secured a victory from the Pulivendla constituency. On the personal front, he is married to Y S Bharathi, and together they have two daughters. He faces 26 criminal cases. View More Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy Personal Life Full Name Y. S. Subsequently, in 2017, he faced arrest once more in a corruption case, although he was ultimately acquitted by the court. 4. In September 2024, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu accused former CM YS Jagan Mohan Reddy of permitting non-sacred activities at the Tirupati Temple during his five-year tenure. Naidu further alleged that Reddy appointed individuals close to him as members of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) board and held him responsible for the supply of adulterated ghee for the temple’s prasadam. He sparked a political controversy by claiming that animal fats were discovered in the ghee used for preparing the sacred prasad. Additionally, Naidu announced the formation of an SIT to investigate the alleged use of animal fats. Political Timeline of Y. S. YSRCP bagged 151 of the 175 seats in the Assembly. 2019 : He was sworn in as the second Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh after its bifurcation in 2014. 2014 : He was elected as MLA. 2011 : On 13 June, he was re-elected to the 15th Lok Sabha in a bye-election. 2011 : He formed a new party YSR Congress (Yuvajana Shramika Raithu Congress Party), on 16th February 2011. 2010 : He resigned from the 15th Lok Sabha. 2009 : He became a Member of the Committee in Finance. 2009 : He was elected as a Parliament member of Kadapa from the Indian National Congress party. 2004 : Jagan started his political life by campaigning for the Congress party in the 2004 elections in Kadapa District. sources.evidenceText: Andhra News Latest News Politics Mood Of AP: YS Jagan Leads CM Race A recent “Mood of Andhra Pradesh” survey dated August 20, 2026, conducted by the IITians Group Hyderabad, has revealed an interesting picture of public preference… venkat Aug 23, 202600:57 am IST Chandrababu NaiduIITians GroupMood Of Andhra PradeshNara LokeshPawan KalyanYS Jagan Mohan Reddy --> A recent “Mood of Andhra Pradesh” survey dated August 20, 2026, conducted by the IITians Group Hyderabad, has revealed an interesting picture of public preference for the next Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh. The survey asked respondents whom they would like to see as the next CM after the upcoming Assembly elections. According to the figures, Y S Jagan Mohan Reddy leads the preference chart with 44 percent support. Nara Chandrababu Naidu stands second with 32 percent. Jana Sena chief Pawan Kalyan gets 6 percent, while Nara Lokesh receives 5 percent support. Meanwhile, 2 percent of respondents opted for “Others,” while 11 percent said they could not say whom they preferred. The numbers indicate a significant lead for Jagan over Chandrababu in this particular survey, with a 12-percentage-point gap between the two leaders. However, these figures should be viewed only as a snapshot of public sentiment at this stage and not as a prediction of the eventual election result. Political alliances, governance, campaign strategies, local issues and changing voter preferences could significantly influence the final outcome. Still, the survey provides an interesting indication of the current mood in Andhra Pradesh with huge anti incumbency in place. sources.evidenceText: Jagan: Jagan completes five years as chief minister of AP | Vijayawada News - Times of India Edition IN IN US Sign In TOI City vijayawada mumbai delhi bengaluru Hyderabad kolkata chennai agra agartala ahmedabad ajmer allahabad amaravati amritsar aurangabad bareilly bhubaneswar bhopal chandigarh coimbatore cuttack dehradun erode faridabad ghaziabad goa gurgaon guwahati hubballi imphal indore itanagar jaipur jammu jamshedpur jodhpur kanpur kochi kohima kolhapur kozhikode ludhiana lucknow madurai mangaluru meerut mumbai region mysuru nagpur nashik navi mumbai noida patna puducherry pune raipur rajkot ranchi thane salem shillong shimla srinagar surat trichy thiruvananthapuram udaipur vadodara varanasi visakhapatnam photos Web Stories Today's ePaper weather andhra elections News City News vijayawada News Jagan completes five years as chief minister of AP Trending Kolkata Doctor Rape Goa European Girl Rape Narendra Modi Noida Visit Sanjauli Mosque Row Gurgaon Delhi Route Closure Shivajinagar Metro Station Kolkata Doctor Rape Goa European Girl Rape Narendra Modi Noida Visit Sanjauli Mosque Row Gurgaon Delhi Route Closure Shivajinagar Metro Station Kolkata Doctor Rape Goa European Girl Rape Narendra Modi Noida Visit Sanjauli Mosque Row Gurgaon Delhi Route Closure Shivajinagar Metro Station This story is from May 31, 2024 Jagan completes five years as chief minister of AP Samdani MN / May 31, 2024, 05:04 IST Share AA + Text Size Small Medium Large Follow us Vijayawada: YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has become the first chief minister of Andhra Pradesh to complete five-year term in office on Thursday. Exuding confidence of winning yet another term in the keenly fought elections, Jagan has promised to take AP into the league of developed states in the next five years. In a message posted on the social media platform X, Jagan thanked the God and people for giving their overwhelming mandate in the 2019 elections to bring YSRCP to power. Jagan took oath as chief minister on May 30, 2019 after party swept to the power with 151 seats in the 175-seat assembly. Significantly, Jagan’s father and late chief minister YS Rajasekhara Reddy served full-term in the office as chief minister between 2004-09. Although TDP supremo Chandrababu Naidu served as chief minister thrice in the past, he could not complete full-term of five years on all three occasions. Naidu first became chief minister by dethroning his father-in-law NT Ramarao a year after TDP coming to power in 1995. He served as chief minister for little over four years in the first term between 1995-1999. Curiously, TDP won the second term under Naidu’s leadership in 1999, but Naidu dissolved the assembly about six month before the completion of his term in 2004. Naidu went for advanced polls following a Maoist attack on him near Alipiri on the way to Tirumala shrine. However, Naidu lost 2004 elections and handed over the reins of undivided AP to YS Rajasekhara Reddy-led Congress party. Interestingly, TDP-led NDA had once again won the elections in 2014, post bifurcation of the AP, giving third term for Naidu as CM. Although Naidu technically had his full-term in office, he could not complete the five years as the elections were held in April 11, 2019 and results were declared on May 23. Naidu took oath as chief minister on June 8, 2014 and vacated the seat almost eight days before completion of his five-year term. Jagan’s term, though marked with a few controversies, was pioneer in several remarkable initiatives including appointment of volunteers to door-deliver the govt services to the poor, setting up of village/ward secretariat administrative system, reforms in education with introduction of English medium in public schools, 17 medical colleges in govt sector and disbursement of over 3.5 lakh crore through various welfare schemes consistently throughout the five-year term. We also published the following articles recently Chief minister Siddaramaiah: Ready to hold BBMP elections CM Siddaramaiah plans to hold BBMP and Zilla/Taluk Panchayat elections post Lok Sabha polls. The delayed polls are set to be conducted across all districts after June 4 vote counting. UCC, 'One Nation, One Election' to be implemented in next term: Amit Shah Union home minister Amit Shah announced plans for implementing a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) and 'One Nation, One Election' system if BJP is re-elected, following consultations with stakeholders within five years. UCC, 'One Nation, One Election' to be implemented in next term: Amit Shah Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced plans to implement a Uniform Civil Code and 'One Nation, One Election' within five years if BJP returns to power. The UCC, a long-standing BJP agenda, was recently enacted in Uttarakhand. The capital city of the United States of America is Washington, D.C., formally known as the District of Columbia and commonly referred to as D.C. U.S. State Capitals Below is a comprehensive alphabetical list of the capital cities of the United States, including their state abbreviation codes, official state nicknames, and the order in which each state was admitted to the Union. The United States consists of 50 states, each with its own capital city, serving as the political and administrative hub. Some well-known state capitals include Sacramento (California), Austin (Texas), Albany (New York) and Denver (Colorado). Washington, D.C., the federal capital, functions independently and serves as the political hub of the nation. State capitals often reflect the unique culture, history, and governance of their respective states, with many serving as historical landmarks. One of the most populated and powerful countries in the world, the United States of America is the third largest country, with a total land area of about 3,794,066 square miles (9,833,520 km2). The United States is situated between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, bordered by Canada to the north and Mexico to the south. The nation's capital is Washington DC. The estimated population of the United States of America (USA) is 331,449,281 according to 2020 US census, the United States is also the third most populous country in the world. Almost 79% of the entire American population lives in urban areas. The five most populated cities in the United States are New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix. The United States is a federation of fifty states and one federal district, Washington, District of Columbia. Forty-eight of the fifty states make up the contiguous United States, and Alaska, while still part of the North American continent, is separated from the lower forty-eight by Canada. The fiftieth state, which entered the union most recently, is Hawaii, a chain of islands located in the Pacific Ocean. The United States also possesses five major unincorporated overseas territories: Puerto Rico and the United States Virgin Islands in the Caribbean, American Samoa, Northern Mariana, and the Islands in the Pacific. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters View image in fullscreen A drone view shows mud covering properties after the flash flood in Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterNearly 1,400 missing, mostly tourists, after Nepal-Tibet flash flood kills at least 356Entire villages swept away after glacial collapse triggers flood in mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates Have you been affected by the flash floods? Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi, Sam Jones, Kate Lamb and agencies Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.41 BSTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 04.53 BSTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google Rescuers are searching for nearly 1,400 people, most of them tourists, who are missing after a catastrophic flash flood hit Nepal and Tibet, thundering down valleys, obliterating entire villages and killing at least 356 people.Efforts to locate those missing – including hundreds of people from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and almost 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. Trucks were upended and houses, roads ⁠and power plants swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing. Deadly flash flood hit Nepal and China - cinemagraphRescue teams have found bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people have been transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care. By Thursday morning, the Nepali army had rescued more than 100 people from flood-affected areas by helicopter.David Fisher, the head of the Nepal delegation of the International Federation of the Red Cross, said entire villages and market areas had been wiped out.In the affected areas, houses, trees and vehicles were submerged or buried in mudslides. Helicopters hovered overhead all day, helping to rescue survivors.The power, volume and speed of the surging waters gave little time for anyone to flee. 9:21 ‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestPeople from the hard-hit areas of Nuwakot and Dhading were seen gathering outside a Nepali army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.Police were recording the names of the missing just outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity due to damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was virtually wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives live there. Desperate for information, he travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family.Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border? Read more“There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”Almost 600 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted were 177 from India, 63 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Before and after images showing the glacier’s collapse Before and after images showing the glacier’s collapsePolice in Nepal said 353 ⁠bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border.Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said. View image in fullscreen Damaged section of highway in Nepal after the flash flood. Photograph: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAn initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated a landslide of ice and rock triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 12 miles (20km) north-east of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s national disaster authority said. Experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas.People shared harrowing stories of how they managed to survive. “I started running. Then a wall of water came thundering down as if it was an earthquake,” said Bibek Kumal, a labourer who was working downstream from the worst-hit Rasuwa district, near Nepal’s Himalayan border with China’s Tibet.From his hospital bed, Kumal said the torrent swept him downstream amid mud and debris but he survived by clinging to a mango tree. “Had there been no mango tree, I would ‌have been washed away to death,” he said.Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor who was being treated at a small hospital, said: “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher.“I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take ⁠her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud. Four or five hours later, a helicopter came to rescue me. My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud. She’s gone.” View image in fullscreen Nepali soldiers carrying a survivor of the flash flood. Photograph: Nepal Army/EPAThe United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel to support communities affected by the disaster. The US government said it would provide $500,000 in emergency assistance.Tibet government officials deployed nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as search dogs and speedboats to help the rescue efforts, China’s official Xinhua news agency said.The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, travelled to the affected area on the China-Nepal border on Thursday to oversee search efforts there.Map showing the flooding-affected locations in Nepal and ChinaThe tour company Himalayan Glacier said 47 people, including two children, were missing from one of its groups in Nepal. Among them were 15 Australians, 10 Canadians, nine Nepalis, eight Americans, two Britons, two Singaporeans and one Russian-American dual citizen, its managing director, Sanket Pandey, said.The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with those concerned about their loved ones, and that getting information about the status of missing people remained difficult.Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaFloodingSouth and central AsiaAsia PacificnewsShare Reuse this content
